title: Knowledge Check 1: Lessons 1-5
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 1-5 of the hermes-consultant-intermediate series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: What should set the length of each phase when a multi-week plan is built?
options: The time needed to reach its gate
A fixed allotment of weeks per phase
The consultant's weekly capacity
The order the phases are listed in
questions.explanation: Each phase ends at a gate, so its length is however long it takes to satisfy that gate, not a preassigned block of weeks.

questions.question: Which force most directly limits how fast discovery and design can move?
options: The number of tools and data sources the delivery touches
The model selected for each scheduled task
How fast the client's stakeholders respond
The size of the implementation backlog
questions.explanation: Stakeholders who must answer questions and approve scope control the pace, so review gates should be scheduled around their calendar, not the consultant's.

questions.question: When a plan is sized for a client build, how should review cycles be treated?
options: As a formality that costs almost no calendar time
As a single pass that runs only at the end
As a small step absorbed into the build effort
As a bottleneck to plan several cycles for
questions.explanation: The show, feedback, and revise loop eats real calendar time, so a plan should assume more than one review cycle rather than a single pass.

questions.question: A requirement captures the process as-built when it records which version?
options: The process as written in the official documentation
The process as actually performed in practice
The process the sponsor describes in a meeting
The process the vendor's manual prescribes
questions.explanation: The as-built view is the process as performed, which is what the build must match, because the documented version diverges and breaks on real data.

questions.question: A requirement is not finished until it records what, in addition to the behavior?
options: The cost, the schedule, and the signoff
The risk, the test, and the reviewer
Its rule, exception, and boundary
The model, the tool, and the provider
questions.explanation: A requirement that survives is behavior plus its rule, its exception, and its boundary with an owner; missing any part leaves it untestable or unsafe.

questions.question: What should a well-captured exception tell an agent to do when it cannot resolve a case?
options: Guess the most plausible value and continue
Pause the run until a human is available
Drop the case without any record
Refuse it and flag it for a human
questions.explanation: The exception is where the agent stays safe: on an unresolved case it should refuse or flag rather than invent an answer, so the failure stays visible.

questions.question: What is the main problem with running every task on one model?
options: It makes the provider and env configuration harder to manage
It overpays easy work and underperforms hard work
It caps the number of scheduled jobs the agent can run
It forces every task onto the cheapest available model
questions.explanation: A single default treats trivial and demanding work as equal, so the easy task overpays and the hard task runs on a model too weak for it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an eval suite built from known-good cases?
options: To make every scheduled run finish more quickly
To remove the need for a human to review output
To catch silent regressions when inputs change
To record every command the agent issues in a log
questions.explanation: A fixed set of known-good cases with expected outputs catches the quiet degradation that a rule, data, or model change can introduce.

questions.question: When an unattended run meets a dangerous command and no one is present to approve it, what is the safe default?
options: Approve it automatically so the run completes
Skip the check and log a warning instead
Retry the command on a stronger model
Deny it so the run stops or diverts
questions.explanation: A headless run should fail closed: blocking the command is the safe default, while auto-approval is reserved for a fully trusted, isolated environment.

questions.question: What makes a skill's description effective for a reusable toolkit?
options: It summarizes the full text of the skill
It names the situation that triggers loading it
It lists every supporting file bundled inside the folder
It names the client the skill came from
questions.explanation: The description is the only thing the agent sees when deciding whether to load the skill, so it must name the situation, not the content.

questions.question: When packaging an engagement into a reusable skill, what should you keep?
options: The client's names and specific data formats
The complete record of the original engagement
The transferable core, minus client detail
Only the parts that were difficult to build
questions.explanation: A reusable skill keeps the procedure that transfers and strips the client-specific detail, or the next engagement cannot put it to use.

questions.question: How much should a single reusable skill try to cover?
options: One deliverable or decision procedure
Everything the consultant needs on a project
A whole engagement from start to finish
Every tool the team uses across clients
questions.explanation: A skill scoped to one deliverable or decision stays loadable and easy to route, while a skill covering everything bloats the index and applies poorly.

questions.question: In a complex client environment, what is the right starting move?
options: Design the ideal system, then adapt the environment to it
Map the existing environment, then design to fit it
Replace the old stack with a cleaner one
Ignore constraints until deployment time
questions.explanation: The environment is given and will reject a design that ignores it, so mapping the stack and its constraints comes before designing the delivery.

questions.question: When integrating with an existing stack, which version should the design be built against?
options: The version described in the vendor's documentation
The version in the client's design slides
The version the running system actually exposes
The newest version the vendor offers
questions.explanation: Documented interfaces and running ones diverge, so an integration designed to the docs breaks against the system that actually exists.

questions.question: What does a sandboxed deploy actually guarantee about the agent's behavior?
options: It automatically approves every dangerous command in a run
It removes the need for any guardrails
It grants the agent write access to production
It isolates where the agent runs, not what it does
questions.explanation: Isolation and approval are separate layers: the sandbox controls where the agent runs, and the guardrail set still controls what it may do there.
